title: Esperanto is named after its inventor’s pen name: Doktoro Esperanto, ‘one who hopes’

cover.alt: An oil portrait of L. L. Zamenhof in 1907: a balding man with round glasses and a greying beard, in a black suit and white bow tie, with a small green star on his lapel.

body: L. L. Zamenhof was a Jewish eye doctor from Białystok, then in the Russian Empire, where different communities each spoke their own language and, as he wrote, ‘looked on all the others as enemies’. In the late 1870s and early 1880s he built a language meant to be everyone’s second language, to foster peace and international understanding. On 26 July 1887 he self-published its first textbook, *Unua Libro*, in Russian, under the pseudonym Doktoro Esperanto, ‘one who hopes’. Early learners liked the name so much that it became the language’s own. It is now the world’s most widely spoken constructed auxiliary language, though no one knows how many people speak it.

slides.heading: Match the ending to its job
slides.explanation: Every common noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a. Verbs don’t change for person or number, so one ending does for I, you and they.

slides.alt: A sepia group photograph of hundreds of people in Edwardian dress posed in front of an arched building, captioned in Esperanto: the second international Esperanto congress in Geneva, 1906.
slides.caption: The second international Esperanto congress, Geneva, 1906, in a photo at the Esperanto Museum in Vienna. The first had met in Boulogne-sur-Mer the year before.

slides.label: estimated speakers, depending on who is counting
slides.text: Estimates of native speakers, who grew up with it at home, range from about 1,000 to 2,000.

slides.heading: From one textbook to a world movement
slides.note: The first World Congress met in Boulogne-sur-Mer. Its Wikipedia now has about 390,000 articles.

slides.question: How many countries have adopted Esperanto as an official language?
slides.explanation: No country has adopted it officially, and it is not one of the UN’s six official languages, although UNESCO backed it in its 1954 Montevideo Resolution.
